Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Liam Weber was 32 when he came to treatment, a married man who worked as a tutor, spending his afternoons moving between families’ homes, a small learning center, and online sessions from the spare room of the apartment he shared with his wife. The event he returned to when trying to explain what had happened to him was not a single attack but a months-long period of stalking that had altered the feel of ordinary life. It began after he tried to set firm limits with someone who had become increasingly intrusive. What stayed with him most vividly was the sense that his movements were no longer his own. He would leave a student’s house and notice a motorcycle idling across the street, then hear the same engine again a few blocks later. At first he told himself he was being dramatic, but the repetition wore that explanation down. He started seeing the same figure outside places where he worked, and on more than one evening he had the unmistakable feeling that someone was hanging back just far enough behind him to make doubt possible and certainty impossible. That uncertainty became part of the terror. He never felt he could prove what was happening in the moment, only that his body knew before his mind would allow it.

One encounter stood out sharply. After a tutoring session, Liam heard a motorcycle rev behind him as he walked to his car. When he turned, the rider stayed helmeted and still. Later that night, after he got home, his phone filled with messages written in a tone that was not openly threatening so much as coldly controlled. The next day, when he tried to describe his alarm to someone else, the response was measured and calm, but the hint of irritation in that person’s voice made his chest tighten. Since then, even calm expressions of anger in other people have carried the force of danger for him. A parent frowning and speaking sharply about a child’s grades, a husband and wife arguing in low voices in a kitchen where he is tutoring, even a clipped tone from a colleague can make him feel he is back in that period when other people’s faces seemed to shift without warning. He has come to believe that people are not what they seem and that trust is naïve; in his words, anyone can sound reasonable while meaning harm.

In the months after the stalking, Liam’s world narrowed. He began avoiding unfamiliar places because not knowing the exits, the street layout, or who might be nearby felt intolerably risky. As a tutor, this changed his work in concrete ways. He stopped accepting new in-home clients in neighborhoods he did not already know, turned down referrals that would have required evening travel, and pushed more sessions online, telling people it was for scheduling efficiency. His income dipped, and he felt humiliated by how relieved he was to stay home. Yet home did not feel entirely safe either. He had trouble falling asleep and, when he did sleep, he woke easily, alert to sounds in the street. A motorcycle passing outside after midnight could bring him upright in bed before he knew what he had heard. During the day he often reacted as if danger were present even when nothing was wrong: footsteps behind him on the sidewalk, a phone notification, a stranger pausing too long near his car. He recognized, sometimes seconds later, that he had jolted or turned or scanned the area before he had any evidence at all.

Liam also found himself avoiding states he used to value. Relaxing felt dangerous, as though letting his guard down invited harm. He stopped reading for pleasure in the evenings, stopped taking long showers, stopped letting himself drift on the couch with his wife after dinner. If she suggested a weekend away or even a spontaneous outing, he would tense and say he would rather stick to familiar routines. Emotional closeness became difficult in the same way. He loved his wife and did not doubt that, but being open, affectionate, or unguarded left him feeling exposed. He would pull back from conversations that might lead to vulnerability, then hate himself for doing it. At his lowest moments he told himself he deserved to suffer because of what had happened, as though being vigilant and unhappy were a fitting penalty for not having handled things better. He was increasingly certain he could not trust himself to do the right thing. If he had acted sooner, been firmer, noticed more, chosen differently—these thoughts looped through him without resolution.

By the time he sought help, the strain was showing in his marriage and work. His wife had begun to say she missed him even when he was sitting beside her. He had started checking behind him on the walk from his car to the learning center and choosing routes based less on convenience than on whether he could see who was approaching. What finally brought him in was a recent moment after a tutoring session when he heard a motorcycle somewhere down the block, spun around so abruptly that he frightened one of his students, and then could not stop shaking. He said he was tired of living as if danger might step out from any corner, tired of distrusting everyone, tired of feeling that rest itself was unsafe. What frightened him most was the idea that this was now his permanent way of being; what he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was to be able to move through a day without bracing for pursuit.
